subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Open your eyes in the morning and the first thing you meet is light. The strong equatorial sun climbs over the acacia trees, spills across the savanna, and paints long shadows on the ground. By the time you eat your breakfast of canjeero, those shadows have already begun to shrink. Light is everywhere in your day, and yet it is so ordinary that we hardly ever stop to ask what it really is. In this unit you are going to stop and look closely.

outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to:
Name light sources and sort them into natural (the sun, stars, fire, lightning) and artificial (torches, lamps, phone screens, car headlights).
Explain that we need light to see, and describe what happens to your eyes in complete darkness.
Explain that light travels in straight lines and use this idea to say where a shadow will fall.
Describe how a shadow forms when an opaque object blocks light.
Sort materials into transparent, translucent, and opaque by testing them with a torch.
Change the size of a shadow on purpose by moving the object or the light, and explain why it changes.
Predict how shadows change through the day and connect this to the sun’s apparent movement across the sky.
Describe reflection — how light bounces off shiny surfaces such as a mirror or still water.
Here are the important words for this unit. Read them now, then come back whenever you meet one in the lesson and it feels fuzzy.

concepts.title: We Need Light to See
concepts.explanation:
Imagine you wake up in the middle of the night, long before the dawn prayer. The room is completely dark. You know your slippers are on the floor, and your water cup is on the shelf, but you cannot see them at all. Now you switch on a torch. Suddenly the slippers and the cup jump into view. What changed? The objects did not move or appear from nowhere. The only thing that changed was that light was now present.

This tells us something surprising: we do not see objects on their own — we see the light that comes from them. For an object to be seen, light must travel from a light source, hit the object, and then bounce off it into your eyes. In a completely dark room there is no light to bounce, so there is nothing for your eyes to catch, and you see only blackness. Your eyes are not broken in the dark; they simply have no light to work with.

Some objects, like the sun or a torch, make their own light. We call these light sources. Most objects around you — a mango, a wooden stool, your brother’s face — do not make their own light. You only see them because light from a source lands on them and reflects into your eyes. This is why the moon can look so bright at night during Ramadan even though the moon makes no light of its own: it is simply reflecting the light of the sun back down to us.

This is why light is so precious to us. Without it, the whole busy world around you would be hidden. You could not see the faces of your family, the colours of a ripe mango, the path to the well, or the words on this page. Everything you enjoy looking at — the blue of the Indian Ocean, the green after the rains, the flight of a flamingo over the water — reaches you only because light carries the picture to your eyes. When you understand that seeing depends completely on light, you begin to notice just how much of a gift it is.

🌟 Did You Know? Light is astonishingly fast. It travels about 300,000 kilometres in a single second. Sunlight leaves the sun and races across space for about eight minutes before it reaches your face. So the sunlight warming you now actually left the sun eight minutes ago!

Let us sort light sources into two families. Natural light sources are not made by people. The greatest of these is the sun, the star that gives Earth almost all of its light and heat. Other natural sources include the distant stars, the flames of a wood fire, and the sudden flash of lightning in a rainy-season storm. Artificial light sources are made by people so that we can see when natural light is not enough: a torch, an oil lantern, an electric lamp, a car headlight, and even the glowing screen of a phone or tablet.

You might wonder about the moon. On a clear night the moon can be bright enough to walk by, so is it a light source? No. The moon is not a light source at all, because it does not make its own light. It is a giant ball of rock that reflects sunlight down to us. We will return to reflection later in this unit.
concepts.example: Think about how much your day is shaped by light sources. Before the sun rises, your family might use a torch or a lantern to move around the house and prepare for the dawn prayer. Once the strong equatorial sun climbs into the sky, it gives so much free light and warmth that no torch is needed at all. When the sun sets quickly, as it does near the equator, the darkness comes fast, and artificial light sources take over again for the evening. Fishermen returning to the Indian Ocean coast, families sharing bariis after dark, and children finishing their reading all depend on artificial light once the great natural light source has gone down. Understanding where light comes from helps you understand the whole rhythm of a day.

concepts.title: Light Travels in Straight Lines
concepts.explanation:
Here is one of the most important ideas in the whole unit, and it is beautifully simple: light always travels in straight lines. It never bends around a corner on its own. Once light leaves a source, it shoots out in perfectly straight paths that scientists call rays, and it keeps going straight until it hits something.

You have seen proof of this many times. When the morning sun shines through a small gap in the roof or between the branches of a tree, you can sometimes see a straight beam of light with dust dancing inside it. That beam is dead straight, not curved. When a car’s headlights sweep across the road at night, the light reaches out in straight lines ahead of the car. If you shine a torch at a wall in a dark room, the light travels in a straight line from the torch to the wall.

Why does this matter so much? Because the straight-line rule is the secret that explains every shadow you have ever seen. Since light cannot bend around an object, anything solid that stands in the path of the light will block it, and the space behind that object stays dark. That dark space is a shadow. Hold on to this rule — light goes straight — and you will be able to work out where any shadow will appear.

You can test the straight-line rule for yourself with a simple trick. Take three small cards and make a tiny hole in the middle of each one. Line the three cards up in a row so the holes are at the same height, and shine a torch through them. The light only reaches your eye on the far side when all three holes are lined up in a perfectly straight line. The moment you slide one card sideways, the beam is blocked and the light disappears. This happens because light cannot bend through the crooked path — it can only pass when the holes make a straight road for it. Scientists have used experiments just like this for hundreds of years to prove that light really does travel straight.
concepts.example: 🌟 Did You Know? Because light travels in straight lines, you cannot see around corners. This is exactly why you cannot see who is coming down a path hidden behind a house until they step into view. Your eyes can only receive light that reaches them in a straight line.

concepts.title: How Shadows Are Born
concepts.explanation:
A shadow is simply a dark shape where light has been blocked. Put three things together and you will always get a shadow: a light source, an object that blocks the light, and a surface for the shadow to fall on. Think of an acacia tree at midday. The sun is the light source. The thick leaves and branches of the tree are the object. The ground is the surface where the cool patch of shade appears. Goats and camels crowd into that shade to escape the fierce heat.

The shadow always forms on the opposite side of the object from the light source. This makes perfect sense once you remember that light travels in straight lines. The light hits the front of the object and is blocked. It cannot curve around to the back, so the back of the object, and the surface behind it, stay dark. If the sun is in the east in the morning, tree shadows stretch out towards the west. As the sun crosses to the west in the evening, the shadows swing round to point east. The shadow always runs away from the light.

Shadows come in different strengths depending on the light. On a bright, cloudless day the equatorial sun makes shadows that are dark and have sharp, clear edges — you can trace the exact outline of a person or a tree on the ground. On a cloudy day the light is scattered and softer, so shadows become pale and their edges turn fuzzy. Indoors, a single small torch makes a crisp shadow, while a big lamp or a room with many lights makes shadows that are faint and blurry, because light arrives from several directions and fills in some of the darkness. Watching how sharp or soft a shadow is can actually tell you something about the light that made it.
concepts.example: There is one more important condition. For a full, dark shadow to form, the object must be opaque — it must block light completely. Your own body is opaque, so you cast a clear shadow on a sunny day. A camel is opaque, a wall is opaque, a closed door is opaque. But a clear glass of water blocks almost no light, so it makes hardly any shadow at all. This is why the kind of material an object is made of matters so much, and it leads us straight to our next big idea.

concepts.title: Three Families of Materials
concepts.explanation:
Not every material treats light the same way. When light meets a material, one of three things happens, and this lets us sort all materials into three families.

Transparent materials let light pass straight through them, so you can see clearly through to the other side. Clear glass, a clear plastic bottle, and clean water are transparent. When you look through the window of a shop in Hargeisa, you can see everything inside because the glass is transparent. Because transparent materials let almost all the light through, they cast only a very faint shadow, or none at all.

Translucent materials let some light through but scatter it, so the light becomes blurry and you cannot see a clear picture through them. Frosted glass, tissue paper, a thin cotton curtain, and a plastic bag are translucent. When sunlight passes through a thin curtain, the room glows with a soft light, but you cannot see the details of what is outside. Translucent materials make faint, fuzzy shadows.

Opaque materials block light completely. No light passes through, so you cannot see through them at all, and they cast the darkest, clearest shadows. Wood, metal, cardboard, a stone, a camel, and your own body are all opaque. The mud-brick wall of a house is opaque, which is why it casts a strong, cool shadow you can sit in during the heat of the day.

🌟 Did You Know? The same material can seem different depending on how thick it is. A single sheet of paper is translucent — hold it up to a lamp and you will see the glow through it. Stack fifty sheets together and the pile becomes opaque, because now the light cannot fight its way through.

You meet all three families every day without even thinking about it. When you pour clean water into a clear glass, you can see straight through both the glass and the water — both are transparent. When the morning light comes softly through a thin cotton curtain and fills the room with a gentle glow, that curtain is translucent. When you shelter from the fierce afternoon sun behind the mud-brick wall of a house, that wall is opaque and gives you a strong, cool shadow to sit in. The same three families explain why a camel standing in the sun casts a sharp dark shadow while a bottle of water beside it barely casts one at all. Once you start naming the families, you will spot them everywhere.
concepts.example: Understanding these three families helps people make good choices. Windows are made of transparent glass so light can flood in and you can see out. A bathroom window might use translucent frosted glass so light still enters but no one can see through it — light and privacy at the same time. A door is made of opaque wood or metal to block both light and view. Every one of these choices depends on how the material treats light.

concepts.title: Making Shadows Grow and Shrink
concepts.explanation:
Shadows are not fixed. You can make the very same object cast a tiny shadow or a giant one, just by moving things around. There are two main ways to change the size of a shadow, and both come back to the straight-line rule.

Moving the object closer to the light makes the shadow bigger. When you hold your hand close to a torch, your hand blocks a wide fan of the spreading light rays, and it throws a large shadow on the far wall. As you move your hand away from the torch and towards the wall, the shadow shrinks. So: close to the light means a big shadow; close to the wall means a small shadow.

Moving the light source changes the shadow too. Bring a torch very close to an object and the shadow swells; pull the torch far back and the shadow becomes smaller and sharper. The angle of the light also matters. When light shines from low down and to the side — the way the early-morning or late-afternoon sun does — shadows stretch out long. When light shines from high overhead, the way the sun does at noon, shadows are short and squat.

Scientists record measurements in tables so they can spot patterns. Halima set a torch at one end of a table and shone it at a wall. She put a small wooden block in the beam and measured the height of its shadow as she moved the block to different distances from the light. Here is what she recorded.

Step 1 — Read the table carefully. Notice that as the number in the first column gets bigger, the number in the second column gets smaller. The block is moving further from the torch, and the shadow is getting shorter each time.

Step 2 — Describe the pattern in words. As the object moves away from the light source (and closer to the wall), its shadow gets smaller. This matches Big Idea 5: close to the light gives a big shadow, far from the light gives a small one.

Step 3 — Make a prediction. The gaps between the shadow sizes are getting smaller (15, 10, 8, 6). If Halima moved the block to 50 cm, the shadow would be a little smaller than 6 cm — a sensible guess is about 5 cm. Making a prediction from a pattern is exactly how real scientists think.

The angle of the light also matters. When light shines from low down and to the side — the way the early-morning or late-afternoon sun does — shadows stretch out long. When light shines from high overhead, the way the sun does at noon, shadows are short and squat.

concepts.title: Shadows Through the Day and the Sundial
concepts.explanation:
Go outside on a sunny day and watch your own shadow from breakfast until sunset, and you will see it perform an amazing slow dance. Early in the morning, when the sun is low in the eastern sky, your shadow is very long and points towards the west. As the morning goes on and the sun climbs higher, your shadow gets shorter. Around noon, when the sun is almost directly overhead — something that happens strongly near the equator where you live — your shadow is at its shortest. In the afternoon the sun sinks towards the west, your shadow grows long again, and now it points towards the east.

Why does the shadow move? It is not because you move, and it is not because the sun really flies across the sky. It is because the Earth is slowly spinning. As our part of the Earth turns, the sun appears to travel from the eastern horizon at dawn, up high at midday, and down to the western horizon at sunset. Because the sun’s position in the sky keeps changing, the direction and length of every shadow keep changing too.

This daily change in shadows is more than just interesting to watch — it is genuinely useful for the people around you. Herders learn to read the length of a shadow the way you might read a clock. A long shadow in one direction means the morning is still fresh and the animals can graze in comfort. A very short shadow means the sun is high and the heat is at its worst, so it is time to bring the camels and goats into the shade of the acacia trees to rest and cool down. A long shadow stretching the other way means the afternoon is fading and the herd must start the walk home before the fast equatorial darkness arrives. In this way, the movement of a shadow across the ground quietly organises the whole working day.

People have used this steady, reliable movement to tell the time for thousands of years. A sundial is a simple clock that works with a shadow. Push a straight stick upright into the sand and watch the shadow it casts. As the day goes on, the shadow sweeps slowly around like the hand of a clock. Mark where the shadow falls each hour, and you have made a working sundial — no battery needed, only the sun. Herders and travellers across East Africa have long read the length of shadows to judge how much daylight is left before they must find water and shelter for the night.

🌟 Did You Know? Before clocks and phones existed, the shadow of a tall stick was one of the most trusted ways to tell the time. The shortest shadow of the whole day marks the moment the sun is highest, which is close to the middle of the day.

methods.title: How a Shadow Is Born
methods.example: To find out where a shadow forms when an object blocks the light from a torch.
steps: Darken the room by closing the curtains.
Stand the object about 20 cm in front of the wall.
Shine the torch at the object from the far side, so the object sits between the torch and the wall.
Look at the wall. Find the dark shadow and notice which side of the object it is on.
Move the torch to the left, then to the right, and watch how the shadow moves.

methods.title: Growing and Shrinking Shadows
methods.example: To find out how the size of a shadow changes when you move the object between the torch and the wall.
steps: Darken the room and shine the torch at the wall.
Hold the object halfway between the torch and the wall. Measure the height of its shadow with the ruler and record it.
Move the object close to the torch. Measure the shadow again.
Move the object close to the wall. Measure the shadow one more time.
Keep the torch still the whole time so the test is fair.

methods.title: The Three Material Families
methods.example: To sort household materials into transparent, translucent, and opaque by testing how much light passes through each one.
steps: Darken the room.
Hold each material in front of the torch, one at a time.
Look at how much light comes through, and whether you can see the torch clearly, dimly, or not at all.
Sort each material into transparent, translucent, or opaque.

methods.title: Make Your Own Sundial
methods.example: To track how an outdoor shadow changes through the day and use it to tell the time, like a sundial.
steps: Early in the morning, push the stick upright into the ground so it stands firmly.
Place a stone at the tip of its shadow. Measure the shadow’s length and write down the time.
Come back every two hours — mid-morning, noon, and afternoon — and mark the new shadow tip with a stone each time.
Measure the shadow at each visit and record the length, the time, and the direction it points.

methods.title: Bouncing Light with a Mirror
methods.example: To explore how light reflects off a mirror and other surfaces.
steps: In a darkened room, shine the torch at the mirror and watch where the light bounces to. Aim the reflected spot onto a wall.
Try to catch the reflected light and move it around the room by tilting the mirror.
Now look at your own reflection in the mirror, the spoon, the water, and the cloth.
Note which surfaces reflect a clear picture and which do not.

activities.title: How a Shadow Is Born
activities.materials: A torch (or a phone torch); A solid object such as a tin can, a mug, or a toy camel; A pale wall or a white sheet; A darkened room
steps: Darken the room by closing the curtains.
Stand the object about 20 cm in front of the wall.
Shine the torch at the object from the far side, so the object sits between the torch and the wall.
Look at the wall. Find the dark shadow and notice which side of the object it is on.
Move the torch to the left, then to the right, and watch how the shadow moves.

activities.title: Growing and Shrinking Shadows
activities.materials: A torch; A small object (a toy, a bottle cap, a spoon); A pale wall; A ruler or measuring tape
steps: Darken the room and shine the torch at the wall.
Hold the object halfway between the torch and the wall. Measure the height of its shadow with the ruler and record it.
Move the object close to the torch. Measure the shadow again.
Move the object close to the wall. Measure the shadow one more time.
Keep the torch still the whole time so the test is fair.
Safety: Small objects must never go in your mouth, nose or ears. Keep them away from babies and toddlers.

activities.title: The Three Material Families
activities.materials: A torch; A clear plastic bag or bottle; Tissue paper or a thin cloth; Cardboard; Aluminium foil; A drinking glass of water
steps: Darken the room.
Hold each material in front of the torch, one at a time.
Look at how much light comes through, and whether you can see the torch clearly, dimly, or not at all.
Sort each material into transparent, translucent, or opaque.
Safety: Plastic bags are not toys — never put them over or near your face.

activities.title: Make Your Own Sundial
activities.materials: A straight stick, about as long as your arm; A sunny patch of open ground or sand; Small stones or chalk to mark the shadow; A measuring tape; A watch or clock to note the time
steps: Early in the morning, push the stick upright into the ground so it stands firmly.
Place a stone at the tip of its shadow. Measure the shadow’s length and write down the time.
Come back every two hours — mid-morning, noon, and afternoon — and mark the new shadow tip with a stone each time.
Measure the shadow at each visit and record the length, the time, and the direction it points.
Safety: Small objects must never go in your mouth, nose or ears. Keep them away from babies and toddlers. Never look directly at the sun — it can damage your eyes.

activities.title: Bouncing Light with a Mirror
activities.materials: A small mirror; A metal spoon; A bowl of still water; A piece of cloth; A torch
steps: In a darkened room, shine the torch at the mirror and watch where the light bounces to. Aim the reflected spot onto a wall.
Try to catch the reflected light and move it around the room by tilting the mirror.
Now look at your own reflection in the mirror, the spoon, the water, and the cloth.
Note which surfaces reflect a clear picture and which do not.
Safety: Glass breaks — carry jars and mirrors with two hands, and tell an adult straight away if anything chips or cracks.

activities.title: Observe: Shadows Through the Day and the Sundial
activities.materials: A torch (or a phone torch); A solid object such as a tin can, a mug, or a toy camel; A pale wall or a white sheet; A darkened room
steps: Look for an example of shadows through the day and the sundial around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Light and Light source.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

terms: Light
Energy that lets us see. Travels in straight lines; can be reflected.
Light source
An object that makes its own light (sun, torch, candle, phone screen).
Natural light source
A light source not made by people (sun, stars, fire, lightning).
Artificial light source
A light source made by people (torch, lamp, headlight).
Shadow
A dark area made when an opaque object blocks light.
Opaque
Blocks light completely; you cannot see through it (wood, metal, cardboard).
Transparent
Lets light through clearly; you can see through it (clear glass, water).
Translucent
Lets some light through but scatters it (frosted glass, tissue paper).
Reflect
When light bounces off a surface (mirror, still water).
Sundial
A tool that tells time using the moving shadow of a stick.

realProblems.prompt: A herder near Garissa wants his goats to rest out of the midday heat. Explain, using the word opaque, why the shade of an acacia tree keeps the ground cool.
realProblems.answer: ✅ Section D Answers 1. The leaves and branches of the acacia are opaque, so they block the sunlight. The ground behind them stays in shadow, which keeps it cool for the goats. 2. Put the torch close to the toy and the toy far from the wall, with the wall well behind it. A close light and a distant wall make the shadow spread out to its biggest. 3. Translucent material such as frosted glass. It lets daylight through but scatters it, so light gets in while neighbours cannot see clearly inside. 4. He can push the stick upright and watch its shadow. A long shadow means morning or late afternoon; the shortest shadow means it is near midday. The direction of the shadow also tells him roughly how far through the day it is. 5. The moon reflects the sun’s light back to Earth. Even the thin new moon catches some sunlight, and that reflected light reaches our eyes, so we see it.

realProblems.prompt: Halima shines a torch on a block. She measures a shadow of 15 cm when the block is 10 cm from the torch, and 6 cm when it is 40 cm away. Predict the shadow size if the block is 50 cm away, and explain your reasoning.
realProblems.answer: ✅ Section E Answers 1. About 5 cm. The shadow keeps shrinking as the block moves away, and the changes are getting smaller (15, then 6 at 40 cm), so at 50 cm it will be a little smaller than 6 cm — roughly 5 cm. 2. Two shadows. Each light source is blocked separately by the can, so each one makes its own shadow on the opposite side. 3. One sheet is thin enough to be translucent, letting some light glow through. A thick stack blocks the light completely, so together the sheets act as an opaque object. Thickness changes how much light gets through. 4. Light travels only in straight lines, so light from the hidden person cannot bend around the corner to reach your eyes. Only when they step into view can light travel in a straight line from them to you.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name two natural and two artificial light sources.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: ✅ Section B Answers 1. Natural: the sun, stars, fire, lightning (any two). Artificial: torch, lamp, car headlight, phone screen (any two). 2. There is no light in the room, so no light can bounce off objects into your eyes. Your eyes need light to see. 3. Light travels in straight lines from a source. When an opaque object blocks the light, the area behind it stays dark. That dark area is the shadow. 4. A translucent material lets some light through but scatters it, so you cannot see clearly. An opaque material blocks light completely, so you cannot see through it at all. 5. Move the object away from the light and closer to the wall (or move the torch further back). 6. In the early morning the sun is low in the sky, so the light comes from the side and stretches the shadow out long. 7. Reflection is when light bounces off a surface. Example: light bouncing off a mirror or still water so you see a picture of yourself. 8. The moon reflects sunlight down to Earth. It makes no light of its own, but the sunlight bouncing off it reaches our eyes.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit, you will be able to:
I can name light sources and sort them into natural (the sun, stars, fire, lightning) and artificial (torches, lamps, phone screens, car headlights).
I can explain that we need light to see, and describe what happens to your eyes in complete darkness.
I can explain that light travels in straight lines and use this idea to say where a shadow will fall.
I can describe how a shadow forms when an opaque object blocks light.
I can sort materials into transparent, translucent, and opaque by testing them with a torch.
I can change the size of a shadow on purpose by moving the object or the light, and explain why it changes.
I can predict how shadows change through the day and connect this to the sun’s apparent movement across the sky.
